properties.entry: Fungi
Neither plants nor animals: fungi feed by breaking down what others leave behind, through a web of fine threads, the mycelium. They are closer relatives of animals than of plants.
Club fungi
The fungi of most mushrooms, toadstools and brackets, which carry their spores on tiny clubs, the basidia.
Fly agaric
The red toadstool with white spots of fairy tales. It is poisonous, and lives in partnership with the roots of birches and pines.
Porcini
A prized edible mushroom with a thick stem and a brown cap, gathered in the woods of Europe every autumn.
Dark honey fungus
One of the largest living things on Earth: a single fungus in Oregon spreads under almost 10 square kilometres of forest, and may be thousands of years old.
Sac fungi
The largest group of fungi, which form their spores in small sacs. It holds yeasts, moulds, morels and truffles.
Baker's yeast
A single-celled fungus that has raised bread and brewed beer and wine for thousands of years, turning sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide.
Penicillium
The blue-green mould in which Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, the first antibiotic.
Black truffle
A fungus that fruits underground among the roots of oaks and hazels, found with the help of trained dogs, and one of the most expensive foods in the world.
Prototaxites
A giant of the first land: trunks up to 8 metres tall, long taken for trees, that were most likely an enormous fungus, when plants were still small.
Animals
Many-celled living things that eat other living things, and most of which move about. They appeared in the seas more than 550 million years ago.
Ediacaran animals
The earliest large animals known, soft-bodied creatures of the sea floor, shaped like fronds, discs and quilts, before the Cambrian.
Charnia
A frond anchored to the deep sea floor, first found in England by a schoolboy in 1957; for long it was thought to be a plant.
Dickinsonia
A flat, ribbed oval up to a metre long. Traces of cholesterol in its fossils show that it was an animal, one of the oldest known.
Cambrian animals
The animals of the Cambrian explosion, when most of the great groups of animals appeared in a few million years, many of them preserved in the Burgess Shale of Canada.
Anomalocaris
The top predator of the Cambrian seas, up to about half a metre long, which swam with flaps along its sides and seized its prey with two spiny arms.
Opabinia
An animal with five eyes on stalks and a long, clawed nozzle on its head, which made the scientists who first saw it laugh.
Hallucigenia
A small worm with legs and spines on its back, so strange that it was first drawn upside down and back to front.
Arthropods
Animals with jointed legs and a hard outer skeleton: insects, spiders, crustaceans and the extinct trilobites. More than three quarters of the known animals are arthropods.
Paradoxides
One of the largest trilobites, up to 37 centimetres long, from the seas of the Cambrian. Trilobites lived for almost 300 million years.
Meganeura
A griffinfly like a dragonfly, with wings 70 centimetres across, one of the largest insects ever, in the forests of the Carboniferous.
Western honey bee
A social insect living in colonies of tens of thousands, which pollinates a third of our crops and tells its sisters where flowers are by dancing.
Vertebrates
Animals with a backbone and a skull: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
Fish
The first vertebrates and still the most numerous: animals of the water that breathe through gills. All the other vertebrates descend from them.
Dunkleosteus
An armoured fish of the Devonian up to 4 metres long, with self-sharpening bony blades in place of teeth and one of the strongest bites ever.
Megalodon
The largest shark ever, perhaps 15 metres or more long, with teeth as big as a hand. It hunted whales.
Coelacanth
A fish with fleshy, limb-like fins, known only from fossils and thought extinct for 66 million years, until one was caught off South Africa in 1938.
Amphibians
The first vertebrates to walk on land, which still lay their eggs in water: frogs, salamanders and caecilians.
Eryops
A heavy amphibian about 2 metres long, with a broad, flat skull, which hunted fish in the swamps like a crocodile.
Axolotl
A salamander of the lakes of Mexico City that never grows up: it keeps its gills all its life, and can regrow lost legs, and even parts of its heart.
Synapsids
The branch of the land vertebrates that leads to the mammals, with one opening in the skull behind each eye. Long before the dinosaurs, they ruled the land.
Dimetrodon
A predator with a great sail on its back, often taken for a dinosaur, though it lived tens of millions of years before them and is closer to us.
Lystrosaurus
A stout plant eater with two tusks, which survived the greatest extinction of all, at the end of the Permian, and then spread over the whole world.
Early mammals
The first mammals and their nearest relatives, mostly small, furry and active at night, which lived in the shadow of the dinosaurs.
Morganucodon
A shrew-sized animal of the Late Triassic, one of the first mammal-like creatures, which hunted insects at night.
Repenomamus
A mammal of China, its larger species as big as a badger, the largest of its time; one was found with the bones of a young dinosaur in its stomach.
Mammals
Warm-blooded vertebrates with hair, which feed their young with milk. After the dinosaurs died out, they grew into every size and way of life.
Platypus
A mammal of Australia that lays eggs, has a duck's bill, finds its prey by electricity, and whose males carry venomous spurs.
Smilodon
The sabre-toothed cat of the Americas, with canines up to 28 centimetres long, thousands of which were trapped in the tar pits of Los Angeles.
Woolly mammoth
An elephant of the Ice Age with a shaggy coat and long curved tusks, hunted by people. The last ones lived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago.
Blue whale
The largest animal that has ever lived, up to 30 metres long and 190 tonnes, which feeds on tiny krill.
Human
An upright ape with a large brain, who appeared in Africa about 300,000 years ago and has since spread over the whole planet.
Reptiles
Vertebrates whose eggs have a shell, so they can be laid on dry land: lizards, snakes, turtles, crocodiles, and the dinosaurs, birds included.
Ichthyosaurus
A marine reptile shaped like a dolphin, which gave birth to live young at sea. Ichthyosaurs were among the first fossil reptiles found, by Mary Anning on the coast of England.
Plesiosaurus
A marine reptile with a long neck, a small head and four flippers, which "flew" through the water. Mary Anning found the first complete one in 1823.
Pterosaurs
Flying reptiles, close relatives of the dinosaurs but not dinosaurs, whose wings were skin stretched from a very long fourth finger.
Pteranodon
A toothless pterosaur with a bony crest and wings up to 7 metres across, which glided over the inland sea of North America catching fish.
Quetzalcoatlus
One of the largest flying animals ever, as tall as a giraffe on the ground, with wings about 10 metres across.
Dinosaurs
Reptiles with legs straight beneath the body, which ruled the land for more than 160 million years. The asteroid of 66 million years ago killed them all but the birds, which are dinosaurs too.
Theropods
The dinosaurs that walked on two legs, with hollow bones, most of them meat eaters, from small feathered hunters to the giants. Birds are theropods.
Tyrannosaurus rex
The "tyrant lizard king": 12 metres long and about 8 tonnes, with the strongest bite of any land animal and tiny arms with two fingers.
Allosaurus
The great hunter of the Jurassic, about 9 metres long, which preyed on stegosaurs and young sauropods in North America.
Spinosaurus
A theropod with a sail on its back and a snout like a crocodile's, longer than T. rex, which hunted fish in the rivers of North Africa.
Velociraptor
A feathered hunter the size of a turkey, with a sickle-shaped claw on each foot, much smaller than in the films.
Birds
The dinosaurs alive today: feathered, toothless, with a beak, and most of them fly. There are more than 10,000 species.
Archaeopteryx
Half bird, half dinosaur: feathers and wings, but also teeth, claws on its hands and a long bony tail. Found in Germany in 1861, two years after Darwin's Origin of Species.
Dodo
A flightless pigeon of Mauritius, about a metre tall, wiped out less than a century after sailors arrived on the island, in the 17th century.
Ostrich
The largest living bird, which cannot fly but runs at 70 kilometres an hour, and lays the largest eggs.
Sauropodomorphs
Plant-eating dinosaurs with long necks and tails, which grew into the sauropods, the largest animals ever to walk the Earth.
Brachiosaurus
A sauropod with front legs longer than its hind legs, carrying its head 9 metres above the ground, like a giraffe, to browse the treetops.
Diplodocus
A sauropod about 25 metres long with a whip-like tail. Copies of the skeleton of "Dippy" were given to museums around the world.
Argentinosaurus
One of the largest land animals ever, about 35 metres long and up to 70 tonnes, found in Patagonia.
Ornithischians
The "bird-hipped" dinosaurs, all plant eaters, often armoured, horned or crested: stegosaurs, ankylosaurs, duck-billed and horned dinosaurs. Despite their name, birds do not descend from them.
Stegosaurus
A plant eater with two rows of tall plates along its back and four spikes on its tail, and a very small brain for its size.
Parasaurolophus
A duck-billed dinosaur with a long hollow crest, through which it could call with deep, trumpeting sounds.
Triceratops
A horned dinosaur with three horns and a great bony frill, which lived alongside T. rex until the very end of the Cretaceous.
Ankylosaurus
A dinosaur armoured like a tank, with bony plates over its back and a heavy club at the end of its tail.
Plants
Living things that make their own food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide, and release the oxygen we breathe. They came onto land about 470 million years ago.
Mosses
Small plants without roots, flowers or seeds, which soak up water like a sponge and spread by spores. They are among the oldest land plants.
Peat moss
A moss that builds the peat bogs, holding up to 20 times its weight in water; the peat bogs store more carbon than all the world's forests.
Common haircap moss
One of the tallest mosses, up to 40 centimetres, with stems like tiny fir trees, on moors and in damp woods.
Cooksonia
One of the first plants with a stem able to carry water: a few centimetres tall, forked and leafless, with spore capsules at the tips.
Ferns
Plants with roots and leaves, but without seeds or flowers, which spread by spores. With their relatives they made up the coal forests of the Carboniferous.
Soft tree fern
A fern of Australia with a trunk up to 15 metres tall, crowned with fronds, like the ferns of the age of the dinosaurs.
Horsetails
Living fossils with hollow, jointed stems, the last of a group that grew to trees 20 metres tall in the Carboniferous.
Gymnosperms
Plants with "naked seeds", in cones, not in fruits: conifers, cycads and the ginkgo. They covered the land in the age of the dinosaurs.
Ginkgo
The last of a group of trees as old as the dinosaurs, with fan-shaped leaves. Ginkgos survived the atomic bomb in Hiroshima.
Giant sequoia
The most massive tree on Earth: "General Sherman", in California, is 84 metres tall and more than 2,000 years old.
Wollemi pine
A conifer known only from fossils until fewer than a hundred trees were found in a canyon near Sydney in 1994.
Flowering plants
Plants whose seeds grow inside fruits, after their flowers are pollinated, often by insects. Nine out of ten plant species are flowering plants.
Archaefructus
One of the oldest flowering plants known, a water plant from China with tiny flowers without petals.
English oak
A long-lived tree of Europe, which can grow for a thousand years and feeds hundreds of species of insects, birds and mammals with its acorns and leaves.
Sunflower
A plant from the Americas whose flower head, which follows the sun while it is young, is made of hundreds of small flowers set in spirals.
Bread wheat
A grass farmed for about 10,000 years since the Neolithic, one of the plants that feed humankind.
